components.description: Measurable spaces and generated event collections
components.gap: Source variants of this entry are not preserved on the reader route. Durrett (sec. 1.1, p. 1) defines a sigma-field as a nonempty collection closed under complements and countable unions, derives closure under countable intersections, and states his reason for leaving that property out of the definition (it makes the definition easier to check); he calls (Omega, F) a measurable space because a measure can be put on it. On p. 4 he defines an algebra, also called a field, by closure under complements and binary unions alone, derives closure under binary intersections, and notes that every sigma-algebra is an algebra. Lines 28-37 instead require Omega to belong to the collection, and give neither the source's nonempty form nor its equivalence with the stated form, nor the reason, the synonym field, the derived intersection closure of an algebra, or the remark that a sigma-algebra is an algebra. No file on the route supplies them.

source_evidence.items: sigma-field as a nonempty collection closed under complements and countable unions; countable = finite or countably infinite; closure under countable intersections by De Morgan; reason for omitting that property from the definition; measurable space as a space on which a measure can be put
intersection of sigma-fields over an arbitrary nonempty index set; generated sigma-field
algebra (or field) by closure under complements and binary unions; closure under binary intersections; every sigma-algebra is an algebra

components.gap: Narrowed variant. Durrett's Theorem 1.1.1(ii) (p. 2) states subadditivity in covering form: if A is contained in the union of the A_m, then mu(A) is at most the sum of the mu(A_m), and his proof works with the traces of the A_m on A. Item 2 (lines 111-113) states only the case in which A is the union itself; the covering form is neither stated nor derived (it needs item 1 as a further step that the text does not take). The source names of parts (i) and (ii), monotonicity and subadditivity, are also not attached to the items.

components.gap: Omitted source example with historical and empirical content. Directly after Example 1.1.2 Durrett (p. 3) gives the astragali, dice made from sheep ankle bones that were used in ancient Egypt: the bone comes to rest in one of four positions scored 4, 3, 6 and 1, there is no reason to think the four outcomes equally likely, and four weights p1, p3, p4 and p6 are needed, which is his concrete case requiring this generality. The example and its claims appear neither in this chapter nor in any file on the reader route; the only treatment (def:p15-w02c-p15-002-astragali) is in an untracked file that no driver inputs.

components.gap: Narrowed and omitted source variants. Durrett (pp. 16-17) (a) defines a random variable with values in R* = [-inf, inf] on a domain D in F, measurable for the Borel sets of R* in its usual topology (generated by [-inf, a), (a, b) and (b, inf]); (b) calls X_n almost surely convergent when the set Omega_o on which the limit exists has probability one, with no prescribed limit; (c) sets X_inf = limsup X_n. The entry requires the domain to be Omega (line 237), equips the extended line with the sigma-algebra generated by the rays [-inf, a] without identifying it with the Borel sets of the order topology, and defines almost sure convergence only to a specified real random variable (lines 317-319). Items (b) and (c) appear nowhere in the foundations; the series chapter has to introduce its own convergence set (independent-random-series.tex lines 23-32).

Durrett follows his definition of a discrete distribution with Example 1.2.8, the point mass at 0 given by its distribution function (p. 13), and Example 1.2.9, a distribution function that is a weighted sum of unit steps at all rationals with positive weights summing to one, to show that a discrete distribution function can be quite wild (pp. 13-14). The entry's only example is the waiting law. Neither source example is constructed on the route: probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02b-p15-002.tex lines 292-298 mention Example 1.2.9 by citation, without its formula or a verification.
